notes.claim: Weapons and combatants flowing from the 2011 collapse of Libya triggered the Tuareg insurgency and jihadist takeover of northern Mali
notes.context: Following the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in Libya in 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters formerly in Libyan state service returned to northern Mali with stockpiles of heavy weaponry. In early 2012, the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA) launched an independence rebellion, only to be swiftly sidelined by militant Islamist organizations—including Ansar Dine and Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM)—which imposed harsh sharia governance over Timbuktu, Gao, and Kidal.

notes.claim: French interventions under Operations Serval and Barkhane halted initial advances but failed to arrest the regional expansion of jihadism
notes.context: In January 2013, France initiated Operation Serval to repel an imminent insurgent drive toward Bamako, successfully liberating major northern towns. In 2014, the mission expanded into Operation Barkhane, deploying over 5,000 French soldiers across five Sahelian states (G5 Sahel). However, the kinetic, counter-terrorist focus failed to remedy underlying state corruption and developmental deficits. Insurgent violence metastasized into Burkina Faso and Niger, catalyzing virulent anti-French popular hostility against prolonged foreign military presence.

notes.claim: Cascading military coups in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger culminated in the creation of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES)
notes.context: Widespread popular and military exasperation with chronic insecurity sparked successful putsches in Mali (2020 and 2021 under Col. Assimi Goïta), Burkina Faso (2022 under Capt. Ibrahim Traoré), and Niger (2023 under Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani). The juntas terminated bilateral defense pacts with France, demanded the departure of the UN MINUSMA mission, and formalized a mutual defense pact, the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), in September 2023, subsequently withdrawing from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 2024.

sources.title: Liptako-Gourma Charter establishing the Alliance of Sahel States (AES)

notes.claim: AES nations severed Western security ties to forge comprehensive defense partnerships with Russia (Wagner / Africa Corps)
notes.context: After expelling French troops and US drone bases, the military regimes pivoted decisively toward Moscow. Thousands of paramilitaries from the Wagner Group (rebranded under the Russian Ministry of Defense as 'Africa Corps') were deployed alongside national armies for regime protection and counter-insurgency. However, joint operations drew intense international condemnation, notably following the March 2022 Moura massacre in Mali, where UN human rights investigators verified the summary execution of hundreds of civilians.

notes.claim: Rivalries and terror campaigns by al-Qaeda (JNIM) and Islamic State (ISGS) have internally displaced over 3 million people
notes.context: The central Sahel serves as the battleground for rival extremist coalitions: Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM, al-Qaeda) and Islamic State in the Greater Sahara (ISGS). Their campaigns of village massacres, improvised explosive devices, and economic sieges have produced over 3 million internally displaced persons across Burkina Faso, Mali, and western Niger. Over 10,000 schools have been shuttered due to targeted threats, thrusting millions of vulnerable citizens into catastrophic food insecurity.
